analysis.one_liner: Caps the sulfur allowed in gasoline so every car on the road pollutes less.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by eight senators from both parties, the bill to cut sulfur in gasoline died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have capped sulfur in gasoline at 40 parts per million per gallon, with a 30 ppm average allowed, starting four years after enactment — roughly a tenth of the sulfur in typical American gasoline. Sulfur poisons catalytic converters, so cutting it means every car on the road pollutes less immediately, not just new models. It was referred to the Senate environment committee and never heard from again before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who breathe urban and regional air — especially children, older adults, and people with asthma — would get cleaner air, since the bill's findings credit low-sulfur gasoline with cutting nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, and hydrocarbons across the whole vehicle fleet at once. Drivers benefit because their catalytic converters and emission systems stop being degraded by sulfur. Automakers also gain, because advanced low-emission and fuel-efficient engines they were developing require very low-sulfur fuel to work.

how_it_helps.text: Caps sulfur in gasoline at 40 parts per million per gallon, with an alternative compliance path of up to 80 ppm if the yearly average stays under 30 ppm, effective four years after enactment.

The bill's findings cite joint auto-and-oil industry research showing that cutting sulfur from 330 ppm to 40 ppm reduces hydrocarbon emissions 34%, carbon monoxide 43%, and nitrogen oxides 51% on low-emission vehicles.
Because sulfur damage to emission controls is not fully reversible, a nationwide year-round standard protects cars as they travel across state lines, unlike rules that only affect new model years.
The findings note U.S. gasoline averaged 300-350 ppm sulfur, far above the European Union's approved 150 ppm standard and Japan's 50 ppm standard.
California, the only state that regulated sulfur in all gasoline, credited low-sulfur gasoline with cutting ozone by 10% in the South Coast and 12% in Sacramento in the year after it took effect.
The EPA administrator could set even lower sulfur limits if new research or advanced vehicle technologies showed significant air quality benefits.

analysis.who_pays: Oil refiners bear the main cost: they would need to remove sulfur during refining, which requires equipment and operating expense, though the bill's own findings call the reduction cost-effective and note the technology was already in use. Some of that cost could reach drivers as slightly higher gasoline prices. Retailers and distributors would also face compliance and testing obligations under the new standard.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil refiners, possibly drivers at the pump

drawbacks.text: Refiners would have to absorb the cost of desulfurizing gasoline, and any portion passed through would mean slightly higher prices at the pump for drivers.
The standard would not take effect until four years after enactment, delaying the air quality benefits the bill projects.
The compliance flexibility lets gasoline reach 80 ppm per gallon in any single year as long as the average stays below 30 ppm, so some fuel sold could carry twice the headline limit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and immediate: cleaner air for everyone, longer-lasting emission controls on every car already on the road, and the enabling conditions for cleaner engine technology. The costs fall on a concentrated set of refiners, and the bill's own findings describe the technology as available and the measure as cost-effective, with California's real-world experience showing measurable ozone reductions. The four-year phase-in and the 80 ppm per-gallon flexibility modestly blunt the benefit, but on balance the public gain clearly outweighs the cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate environment committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Moynihan introduced the bill on July 30, 1998, joined by seven original cosponsors, five Democrats and two Republicans, including the Republican senators from Vermont and New York.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil refiners came out ahead: no federal sulfur cap was enacted, so refiners avoided a mandatory desulfurization requirement. The public got nothing — no cleaner gasoline standard came out of this Congress through this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil refiners, who avoided a sulfur cap

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — seven cosponsors split five Democrats and two Republicans — but the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call ever showed a partisan divide.

industries.note: Refiners would have had to remove sulfur from gasoline nationwide, a real capital and operating cost — though the bill's findings say the technology was readily available and in use, and were developed in California. Keeping sulfur in cheap gasoline is what degrades the catalytic converters on every car the public already owns.

Low-sulfur gasoline makes low-emission and ultra-low-emission vehicles work as designed and enables technologies like direct-injection engines and NOx traps the industry was developing; the industry's own joint research is the backbone of the bill's findings. Cleaner fuel helps automakers meet emission standards while also cleaning the air.
They would face new compliance, testing, and recordkeeping duties for the sulfur limits, but would sell the same product to the same customers, with any cost passed through in the price of fuel.
